clue.text: Radical book writer's husband sent packing

indicators.note: a husband sent packing is dismissed, so his letter is taken away from the book's name

parts.note: Esther is a book of the Old Testament, here read as the possessive of the book's name

explanation.surface: A revolutionary author's husband has been thrown out of the house.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sent packing' removes H from ESTHER. 'Radical' here is the old chemical sense, a group of atoms acting as a unit, not a political extremist.
explanation.definitionFit: In older chemistry the compound formed from an acid and an alcohol was spoken of loosely as a radical, a combining group.

clue.text: The Times, perhaps, can be of good report

indicators.note: perhaps hints that the word Times could be some other arrangement

parts.note: to be able is to have the ability, so can be gives able

explanation.surface: A claim that the newspaper can be well regarded.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' makes ESTIM from TIMES, a nod to the newspaper the puzzle appears in.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone of good repute is worthy of esteem and respect.

clue.text: Tie up bunch of flowers

definitions.meaning: to bind tightly, as a bird before cooking
a compact cluster of blooms at the top of a stem

explanation.definitionFit: Both a verb for binding firmly and a botanist's word for a tight head of blooms.

clue.text: Sharp remark about sub-standard driving position

indicators.note: sub means under, and in this down clue the driving position is placed beneath the standard

parts.note: re means about or concerning
par is the standard score on a golf hole
a tee is where a golfer drives from

explanation.surface: A cutting comment about someone's poor driving.
explanation.walkthrough: 'sub-standard' reads as poor, but 'sub' puts TEE under PAR in the down entry. 'driving' is golf, not motoring.
explanation.definitionFit: Quick witty retort or banter; a single sharp riposte is a sample of it.

clue.text: Italian tower affected by a river

parts.note: camp means showily affected or mannered
the Nile is the great African river

explanation.surface: An Italian tower has been damaged by a flooding river.
explanation.walkthrough: 'affected' looks like 'damaged by' but is the adjective CAMP, meaning theatrical and mannered.
explanation.definitionFit: A freestanding bell tower, typically beside an Italian church, goes by this Italian word.

clue.text: The solid figure of a deaconess

indicators.note: of means taken from within, so the letters come from inside deaconess

explanation.surface: A deaconess has a sturdy build.
explanation.walkthrough: 'solid figure' suggests a stout physique; it is a geometrical solid.
explanation.definitionFit: A geometric solid tapering from a circular base to a point.

clue.text: Hawthorn can bear flowers round the bark

parts.note: may means is permitted to, so can
to blossom is to bear flowers, as a tree does all round its bark

explanation.surface: A hawthorn tree bursting into flower all round its trunk.
explanation.walkthrough: May is itself another name for the hawthorn, whose white flowers come in that month.
explanation.definitionFit: The flowering hawthorn shrub of hedgerows, named for the month of its white blooms.

clue.text: A turn about

parts.note: a round is a turn, as in a round of drinks

explanation.surface: Instructions to wheel about.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both mean approximately or in the vicinity.

clue.text: Rat-catcher — the Munich one for a change

indicators.note: for a change says the letters of Munich one are rearranged

explanation.surface: A German-made pest controller, swapped for variety.
explanation.walkthrough: The rat-catcher is the Egyptian mongoose, not a person.
explanation.definitionFit: The Egyptian mongoose, prized for killing rats and snakes, bears this name.

clue.text: Wind from Continental country

parts.note: EUR is an abbreviation for European, of the Continent
the US is the United States

explanation.surface: A breeze blowing in from a mainland European state.
explanation.definitionFit: In Greek myth the god of the east wind, and so that wind itself.

clue.text: Mole's such an honest fellow, said the Prince

definitions.text: Mole's such an honest fellow, said the Prince

parts.words: Mole's such an honest fellow, said the Prince
parts.note: in Hamlet the Prince addresses his father's ghost beneath the stage as old mole and as an honest, trusty fellow

explanation.surface: A prince vouches for the honesty of a burrowing animal.
explanation.walkthrough: The Prince is Hamlet, who calls the ghost moving under the stage 'old mole' and 'truepenny', an old word for a trusty fellow.
explanation.definitionFit: An archaic term for a reliable, straightforward person, used by Shakespeare for the ghost.

clue.text: Whence five banks brought a cargo for Masefield

definitions.text: Whence five banks brought a cargo for Masefield

parts.words: Whence five banks brought a cargo for Masefield
parts.note: five banks of oars make a quinquireme, which in Masefield's poem Cargoes comes from a distant biblical land

explanation.surface: Asks where some financial institutions sent goods to a poet.
explanation.walkthrough: 'five banks' suggests financial institutions; it means five banks of oars, the quinquireme of Nineveh in John Masefield's poem Cargoes, coming from distant Ophir.
explanation.definitionFit: The biblical land of gold, named in the opening line of Masefield's poem as the quinquireme's starting point.

clue.text: Offer to win by losing each round

definitions.text: Offer to win by losing each round

parts.words: Offer to win by losing each round
parts.note: in solo whist a player may bid to take no tricks at all, winning by losing every one

explanation.surface: A paradoxical proposal: victory through defeat in every round of a contest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Offer' is a bid in a card game, and each 'round' is a trick.
explanation.definitionFit: In solo whist this call undertakes to lose every trick, a contract won by losing.

clue.text: The Australian range that Polly sat in?

definitions.meaning: a mountain chain in South Australia named after the navigator Matthew ...
the nursery rhyme's Little Polly sat among the cinders

explanation.surface: A nursery-rhyme girl perched somewhere in the Australian mountains.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags the playful second sense: Polly of the rhyme shares her surname with fragments she might sit among.
explanation.definitionFit: Both the South Australian mountain chain and an old word for small fragments, echoing the nursery rhyme heroine's surname.

clue.text: Woman and husband on the point of being inflexible

parts.note: Ada is a woman's name
a man is a husband, as in man and wife
a tine is a prong or point, as of a fork

explanation.surface: A married couple on the verge of becoming stubborn.
explanation.walkthrough: 'on the point of' looks like 'about to', but 'the point' is TINE and 'on' just joins.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: hard as diamond, unyielding.

clue.text: God with gift for nonsense

parts.note: Balder is the Norse god of light and beauty
dash is a West African word for a tip or present

explanation.surface: A deity bearing a present for rubbish.
explanation.walkthrough: DASH as a gift or tip is a West African usage that the solver may not know.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: both mean senseless talk or rubbish.

clue.text: It ran rings round the old bull

definitions.text: It ran rings round the old bull

parts.words: It ran rings round the old bull
parts.note: the Minotaur of Greek myth was confined in a maze of winding passages built by Daedalus

explanation.surface: Something outmanoeuvred an ageing bull.
explanation.walkthrough: 'ran rings round' means outclassed, but here describes winding corridors encircling the Minotaur of Crete.
explanation.definitionFit: The Cretan maze that enclosed the half-bull Minotaur in Greek legend.

clue.text: First sign of small cage bird

indicators.note: the first sign of a word is its opening letter, here of small

parts.note: a mew is a cage for hawks, especially while moulting

explanation.surface: A small cage bird shows its first sign of life.
explanation.walkthrough: 'cage bird' looks like one phrase, but 'cage' gives MEW and 'bird' alone is the definition.
explanation.definitionFit: A small diving duck of northern Europe and Asia, the male mostly white.

clue.text: This sharpens the wits when set to work

indicators.note: set to work means put into operation, so the letters of when set to are reworked

explanation.surface: Something that keeps the mind keen once it gets going.
explanation.walkthrough: 'set to work' reads as a phrase, but 'when set to' is the fodder and 'work' the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Literally a stone for honing blades, figuratively anything that keeps the mind keen.

clue.text: What thugs do right in street corner

indicators.note: in means one piece goes inside another

parts.note: an angle is a corner

explanation.surface: Muggers lurking on a street corner.
explanation.definitionFit: Garrotters choke victims; violent criminals throttle people.

clue.text: Where to find the end of Napoleon's reputed revolver

definitions.text: Where to find the end of Napoleon's reputed revolver

parts.words: Where to find the end of Napoleon's reputed revolver
parts.note: the revolver is the palindrome Able was I ere I saw ..., attributed to Napoleon, which reads the same either way and ends on his island of exile

explanation.surface: Asks where to find the end of a gun once owned by Napoleon.
explanation.walkthrough: 'revolver' suggests a gun, but means a sentence that turns round on itself: Napoleon's supposed palindrome ends with the island where he was exiled.
explanation.definitionFit: The Mediterranean island of Napoleon's first exile, which closes the famous palindrome credited to him.

clue.text: Introduce the cane, perhaps, in consequence

parts.note: to import is to bring in or introduce

indicators.note: perhaps suggests the word cane might be rearranged into another form

explanation.surface: A suggestion of bringing back corporal punishment, with consequences.
explanation.walkthrough: 'perhaps' turns CANE into ANCE.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: something of consequence has significance or weight.

clue.text: Warehouse in decline

definitions.meaning: a storehouse, especially in South and East Asia
to sink or fall off, as in going downhill

explanation.surface: A warehouse falling into disrepair.
explanation.definitionFit: An Anglo-Indian word for a storage building, and as two words a phrase for sinking or diminishing.

clue.text: The French on Everest, for example, had to get to the top

parts.note: the French word for on is sur
Everest is an example of a mountain, a mount

explanation.surface: A French expedition had to conquer Everest.
explanation.walkthrough: 'The French' wants to be LE, but the phrase means 'the French for on'.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to climb over or conquer by reaching the summit.

clue.text: South African support for native in Israel

parts.note: A is an abbreviation for African
a bra is a supporting undergarment

explanation.surface: A South African gives help to someone born in Israel.
explanation.walkthrough: 'South African' looks like one person; it is S and A separately.
explanation.definitionFit: A Jew born in Israel is called this, after a native prickly pear cactus.

clue.text: Bishop a doubter? What a come-down!

parts.note: B is the chess abbreviation for bishop
Thomas was the doubting apostle; Thos is the short form of his name

explanation.surface: A churchman voices his doubts before a sudden letdown.
explanation.walkthrough: The doubter is Doubting Thomas, abbreviated THOS.
explanation.definitionFit: An anticlimax, a ludicrous drop from the lofty to the trivial, is exactly a come-down.

clue.text: Sloth in hot country written up in verse

indicators.note: in places one piece inside the other

parts.note: H is the abbreviation for hot, as on taps

indicators.note: written up in a down clue means the word is placed upward, reading backwards

parts.note: the UK is the United Kingdom
the ai is a three-toed sloth

explanation.surface: A lazy animal in a hot land written about in poetry.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sloth' looks like laziness but is the three-toed animal of crossword fame; 'written up' works because in a down clue the letters read upward.
explanation.definitionFit: A Japanese verse form of three lines with seventeen syllables.

clue.text: Worthless fellow in dirty film

definitions.meaning: a layer of filth floating on a liquid

explanation.surface: A good-for-nothing actor appearing in a sleazy movie.
explanation.definitionFit: Both a contemptible person and the frothy layer of impurity on a liquid's surface.

clue.text: Gamble to get house in the Army possibly

definitions.text: Gamble to get house in the Army possibly

parts.words: Gamble to get house in the Army possibly
parts.note: house or housey-housey was the services' name for the numbers game, where a full card wins by calling house

explanation.surface: A soldier bets in hope of winning a home.
explanation.walkthrough: 'house' is not a dwelling: it was the military name for the numbers game, and the winning call.
explanation.definitionFit: The numbers game of chance played for money, known in the forces as house.

clue.text: Unidentified coin got in change

indicators.note: change tells us to alter the order of the letters in coin got in

explanation.surface: A coin of unknown origin turned up in someone's change.
explanation.walkthrough: 'change' looks like loose coins, which suits the surface, but is the anagram signal.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone travelling under a false name is unknown, with identity concealed.

clue.text: In error, the man admitted old engineers into the club

indicators.note: admitted means let in, so one piece goes inside the other
in error means mistaken, so the letters of the man are set down wrongly

parts.note: AEU was the Amalgamated Engineering Union, now merged away

explanation.surface: A man was let into the club by mistake, along with some retired engineers.
explanation.walkthrough: 'In error' rearranges THE MAN into ATHENM, and 'admitted' puts AEU inside it. The definition is the London gentlemen's club, or any literary club.
explanation.definitionFit: A London gentlemen's club for literary and learned men, and generally any literary society.

clue.text: Fool not many initially avoid

indicators.note: not means without, so a piece is left out of the word for fool
initially says the omitted letter is the one at the start

parts.note: to delude is to fool or deceive
D is the Roman numeral for 500, a large number

explanation.surface: A fool who avoids not many people at the start.
explanation.walkthrough: 'not' and 'initially' remove the opening D (500, so 'many') from DELUDE.
explanation.definitionFit: Synonym: to evade or escape someone or something.
